question: 理性是在找真相，还是在替我们辩护？
question_en: Does reason seek the truth, or just argue our case?
sub: 结论常常先到、理由随后赶来；可科学与辩论又像是理性在纠正它自己。
sub_en: Conclusions often arrive first and reasons hurry after; yet science and debate look like reason correcting itself.

casting.reason: 他用裂脑实验看见左脑「解释器」当场编理由，认为讲故事是大脑的本职，但故事对不对要由外部世界来判。
casting.reason_en: His split-brain experiments caught the left hemisphere's interpreter inventing reasons on the spot; he holds that storytelling is the brain's job, but the world outside decides whether the story is true.

casting.reason: 他主张理性是激情的奴隶，管不了人想要什么，却能纠正人信错了什么。
casting.reason_en: He holds that reason is the slave of the passions: it can't dictate what we want, but it can correct what we wrongly believe.

casting.reason: 他提出「象与骑象人」，把理性比作替直觉写稿的新闻发言人，又相信观点多样的群体能互相纠错。
casting.reason_en: Author of the elephant-and-rider metaphor, he casts reason as a press secretary writing copy for intuition, yet trusts a genuinely diverse group to correct one another.

casting.reason: 他一生以诘问求真，宁可被驳倒，追问「理性只会辩护」这个结论本身是怎么得来的。
casting.reason_en: A lifelong questioner who would rather be refuted than refute, he asks how the claim that reason only defends was itself arrived at.

casting.reason: 他著《解蔽》，认为毛病不在理而在心被一偏之见遮挡，开出「虚壹而静」和师友相正的方子。
casting.reason_en: Author of 'Dispelling Obscuration', he locates the fault not in reason but in a mind blinded by one corner, and prescribes emptiness, unity and stillness plus correction by teachers and friends.

casting.reason: 他以中观破一切执见，认为立了主张才有要护的东西，发言人正由执见而生。
casting.reason_en: Through Madhyamaka he dismantles every fixed view, arguing that the press secretary is born the moment we stake out a position worth protecting.

casting.reason: 他把科学看作一套专门对付自欺的笨办法，挑战者号调查让他坚信现实必须压过公关。
casting.reason_en: He sees science as a set of clumsy tricks for not fooling yourself, and the Challenger inquiry convinced him that reality must take precedence over public relations.

casting.reason: 他认为每种哲学都是作者的自白、求真也是一种意志，却主张调动更多视角来逼近客观。
casting.reason_en: He holds that every philosophy is its author's confession and the will to truth is itself a will, yet argues that more and different eyes bring us closer to objectivity.

casting.reason: 她用实验测出人对好消息与坏消息更新信念的不对称，关注分歧出现时大脑如何关上耳朵。
casting.reason_en: Her experiments measure how unevenly people update on good news versus bad, and how the brain stops listening once a disagreement appears.

posts.text: 我从六十年代起研究裂脑病人：连接左右脑的胼胝体被切断了。我给病人P.S.的右脑看雪景、左脑看鸡爪，再让他挑图卡。左手（归右脑管）挑了铲子，右手挑了鸡。问他为什么，管语言的左脑根本没见过雪景，却张口就答：「鸡爪配鸡，铲子用来清鸡舍。」毫不迟疑，毫不心虚。我把这套系统叫作解释器。**它的本职不是求真，而是让故事连贯。**
posts.text_en: From the 1960s on I studied split-brain patients, whose corpus callosum, the bundle of fibres joining the two hemispheres, had been cut. I showed one patient, P.S., a snow scene to his right hemisphere and a chicken claw to his left, then had him pick matching cards. His left hand, run by the right hemisphere, chose a shovel; his right hand chose a chicken. Asked why, his left hemisphere, which does the talking and had never seen the snow, answered at once: "The chicken claw goes with the chicken, and you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed." No hesitation, no embarrassment. I call this system the interpreter. **Its job is not truth but a story that hangs together.**

glossary.胼胝体: corpus callosum（胼胝体）：连接左右大脑半球的粗大神经纤维束，切断后两个半球难以直接交换信息。
glossary.解释器: the interpreter（解释器）：加扎尼加对左脑一套机制的称呼，它不断为行为与感受编出说得通的解释，哪怕并不掌握真正的原因。

glossary_en.corpus callosum: The thick bundle of nerve fibres linking the two cerebral hemispheres; once cut, the halves can barely share information directly.
glossary_en.interpreter: Gazzaniga's name for a left-hemisphere system that keeps producing plausible explanations for what we do and feel, even when it has no access to the real cause.

posts.text: 我早说过：**理性是、也应当只是激情的奴隶**。理性自己推不动任何行动，它只告诉你哪条路通向你已经想要的东西，所以加扎尼加的病人一点也不奇怪。但别把话说过头：奴隶也会纠正主人的事实错误。我想吃那只果子，理性告诉我它有毒，欲望随即消散。激情只有建立在错误的假定上、或选错了手段时，才谈得上不合理。理性管不了你要什么，却管得了你信什么。
posts.text_en: I said it long ago: **reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.** Reason on its own moves no one to act; it only tells you which road leads to what you already want, so Gazzaniga's patients don't surprise me in the least. But don't overstate it: a slave can still correct his master's facts. I want that fruit; reason tells me it is poisonous, and the desire falls away. A passion can be called unreasonable only when it rests on a false supposition or picks the wrong means. Reason has no say in what you want, but it has a great deal of say in what you believe.

glossary.激情: passions（激情）：休谟用语，泛指欲望、情感与好恶，是一切行动的动力来源。

glossary_en.passions: Hume's word for desires, emotions and likes and dislikes generally: the source of every motive to act.

posts.text: 我把它比作象与骑象人：直觉是大象，推理是骑象人，他常常不是在指路，而是替大象的去向写新闻稿——**理性更像新闻发言人，而不是法官**。我让人解释，一对兄妹自愿、只发生一次的性关系为什么错，理由逐条被驳倒，他们仍说：「说不清，但就是错。」可梅西耶和斯珀伯补上了另一半：推理本为争论而进化，一个人拿它找自己的理，很差；一群人拿它挑彼此的错，很好。
posts.text_en: I picture it as an elephant and its rider: intuition is the elephant, reasoning is the rider, and often he isn't steering at all but writing press releases for wherever the elephant is headed. **Reason is more like a press secretary than a judge.** I asked people why it's wrong for a brother and sister to have sex once, by mutual choice. Every reason they gave was knocked down, and they still said, "I can't explain it, but it's just wrong." Mercier and Sperber supplied the other half, though: reasoning evolved for arguing. Used alone to find support for yourself, it's poor; used by a group to pick holes in each other's arguments, it's very good.

glossary.象与骑象人: the elephant and the rider（象与骑象人）：海特的比喻，大象代表自动运转的直觉与情绪，骑象人代表有意识的推理。

glossary_en.elephant and its rider: Haidt's metaphor: the elephant stands for automatic intuition and emotion, the rider for conscious reasoning.

posts.text: 诸位说理性只会辩护。可我想问：你们是怎么知道这一点的？加扎尼加做了实验，海特驳倒了受试者的理由，休谟分辨出哪种激情不合理——这难道不都是理性在找真相？我一生只知道一件事：我一无所知。我在雅典街头和人交谈，从不为了赢，而是为了被驳倒。**被驳倒的人得到的比驳倒人的更多，因为他摆脱了一个错误。**所以毛病不在理性，在我们拿它去做什么。
posts.text_en: You all say reason only defends. But let me ask: how do you know that? Gazzaniga ran an experiment, Haidt knocked down his subjects' reasons, Hume worked out which passions are unreasonable. Isn't every one of those reason looking for the truth? I have known only one thing all my life: that I know nothing. I talked with people in the streets of Athens never to win, always to be refuted. **The one who is refuted gains more than the one who refutes, for he is rid of an error.** So the trouble isn't reason; it's what we use it for.

posts.text: **凡人之患，蔽于一曲而暗于大理。**欲为蔽，恶为蔽，始为蔽，终为蔽，远为蔽，近为蔽。此非理之过也，心有所私，则理为之役耳。然心可治：人何以知道？曰心。心何以知？曰虚壹而静。不以所已臧害所将受，谓之虚；不以夫一害此一，谓之壹；不以梦剧乱知，谓之静。治之之术，在学、在师，非恃一人之明。
posts.text_en: **The common affliction of men is to be blinded by one corner and left in the dark about the larger order.** Desire blinds, aversion blinds; seeing only the beginning or only the end, only the far or only the near, all blind. This is no fault of reason: when the mind has private leanings, reason becomes their servant. Yet the mind can be governed. How do we know the Way? Through the mind. How does the mind know? By being empty, unified and still. Not letting what it already holds obstruct what it is about to receive is called emptiness; not letting one thing obstruct another is called unity; not letting dreams and agitation disturb knowing is called stillness. The method lies in study and in teachers, not in relying on one man's brilliance.
posts.vernacular: **人的通病，是被局部的一角蒙蔽，看不清整体的大道理。**欲望会蒙蔽人，厌恶会蒙蔽人；只看开头、只看结尾、只看远处、只看近处，都会蒙蔽人。这不是道理本身的错，而是心里有私，道理就被它差遣了。但心是可以治理的：人靠什么认识道？靠心。心又靠什么认识？靠「虚壹而静」。不让已经装进去的成见妨碍将要接受的新东西，叫虚；不让对这一件事的认识妨碍对那一件事的认识，叫壹；不让胡思乱想和心烦意乱扰乱认知，叫静。治心的办法在于学习、在于老师，而不是只靠一个人的聪明。

glossary.蔽: obscuration（蔽）：荀子用语，指心被一偏之见遮挡，只见局部而不见全体。
glossary.虚壹而静: empty, unified and still（虚壹而静）：荀子的治心之法——不让旧见挡住新知，能同时容纳多种认识，不被杂念扰乱。

glossary_en.empty, unified and still: Xunzi's method for governing the mind: don't let old views block new knowledge, hold several understandings at once, and don't let agitation cloud perception.

posts.text: 诸君所争，皆在理性所护之「见」。吾《中论》言：「大圣说空法，为离诸见故；若复见有空，诸佛所不化。」执一见为最真，即见取见，发言人正由此生。**有所立则有所护，有所护则理为之辩。**故吾《回诤论》曰：「若我宗有者，则我是有过；我宗无有故，如是不得过。」非无言也，破执而不立执耳。
posts.text_en: What you are all fighting over is the view that reason stands guard over. In my Middle Treatise I wrote: "The Great Sage taught emptiness to free people from all views; those who then hold emptiness itself as a view, even the Buddhas cannot help." To cling to one view as the highest truth is attachment to views, and that is where the press secretary is born. **Once you stake out a position you have something to protect, and once you have something to protect, reason starts arguing its case.** So in my Rebuttal of Objections I said: "If I had a thesis, I would be at fault; since I have none, no fault can be found in me." This is not silence. It is breaking one's clinging without setting up a new one.
posts.vernacular: 各位争的，都是理性在保护的那个「见解」。我在《中论》里说：「佛陀讲空，是为了让人脱离一切见解；如果又把『空』当成一个见解抓住，那连诸佛也教化不了。」把某一个见解执为最高真理，就叫见取见，新闻发言人正是从这里生出来的。**一旦立了主张，就有了要保护的东西；有了要保护的东西，理性就开始替它辩护。**所以我在《回诤论》里说：「如果我有自己的主张，我就会有过失；正因为我不立主张，所以挑不出我的过失。」这不是不开口，而是破掉执着，却不再立一个新的执着。

glossary.见取见: attachment to views（见取见，dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa）：佛教所说的烦恼之一，把自己所持的见解当作最高、最真而执守不放。
glossary.空: emptiness（空，śūnyatā）：中观的核心概念，指一切事物都没有独立不变的自性，依条件而成立。

glossary_en.attachment to views: In Buddhist analysis, an affliction: treating the views one holds as the highest and truest, and refusing to let go of them.
glossary_en.emptiness: Śūnyatā, the core idea of Madhyamaka: nothing has an independent, unchanging essence; everything arises from conditions.

posts.text: 我在一次毕业典礼上说过：**第一条原则是你绝不能欺骗自己——而你恰恰是最容易被骗的那个人。**科学不是什么高尚的理性，它是一堆专门对付自欺的笨办法。密立根测电子电荷，数值偏小。后来的人测出更大的数，以为自己错了，就找理由往他的数凑，好些年才一点点爬到正确值。这就是发言人在实验室里上班。解药是：先写下你要怎么判自己错，再去看数据。
posts.text_en: At a commencement once I said: **the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.** Science isn't some noble faculty of reason; it's a pile of clumsy tricks for beating self-deception. Millikan measured the charge on the electron and got a number a bit too low. The people after him got bigger numbers, figured they must be wrong, and looked for reasons to bring them closer to his. It took years to creep up to the right value. That's the press secretary clocking in at the lab. The cure: write down how you'll decide you're wrong before you look at the data.

posts.text: 你们在争理性找不找真相，却从没问过：为什么要真相？**迄今每一种伟大的哲学，都是其作者的自白，一种不自觉的回忆录。**理性向来是某种意志的工具，先替它的需要立法，再给这法披上「客观」的袍子。可别以为我只会拆台。正因为一切认识都出自某个视角，看同一件事的眼睛越多、越不同，我们对它的概念才越完整。客观不是没有立场，而是能调遣许多立场。
posts.text_en: You argue over whether reason finds the truth, and never ask: why truth at all? **Every great philosophy so far has been the self-confession of its author, a kind of involuntary and unconscious memoir.** Reason has always been the tool of some will: it legislates for that will's needs, then drapes the law in the robe of objectivity. But don't think I only tear things down. Precisely because all knowing comes from a perspective, the more eyes, and the more different the eyes, we bring to one thing, the more complete our concept of it. Objectivity is not having no standpoint; it is being able to command many.

glossary.视角: perspective（视角）：尼采视角主义的核心——一切认识都出自某个特定的立场与需要，不存在「从无处看」的知识。

glossary_en.perspective: The core of Nietzsche's perspectivism: all knowledge comes from a particular standpoint and set of needs; there is no view from nowhere.

posts.text: 我做过一个实验：先让人估计自己患癌、离婚的概率，再告诉他们真实数字。真相比预想好，人立刻把估计调过去；真相比预想坏，调整就缩水一大截。好消息照单全收，坏消息打折。卡汉的研究更扎心：同一道统计题，换成枪支管制的话题，**算术越好的人，越会把数据算成自己想要的结论**。这就是动机性推理。聪明不是解药，它只会让发言人更能干。
posts.text_en: In one experiment I had people estimate their chances of getting cancer or divorcing, then told them the real figures. When the truth was better than they'd guessed, they moved their estimate right over; when it was worse, the adjustment shrank by a lot. Good news taken at face value, bad news discounted. Dan Kahan's work stings more: take the same statistics problem, recast it as a question about gun control, and **the better someone is at maths, the more skilfully they compute the answer they wanted.** That's motivated reasoning. Being clever is no cure; it just makes the press secretary better at the job.

glossary.动机性推理: motivated reasoning（动机性推理）：先有想要的结论，再有选择地收集、解读证据去支持它。

glossary_en.motivated reasoning: Starting from the conclusion you want, then selectively gathering and interpreting evidence to support it.

posts.text: @海特 你说一群人互相挑错就能逼近真相。可雅典五百人的陪审团判了我死刑，挑错的人一个也不少。人多只在一个条件下有用：有人肯当牛虻，也有人肯被叮。若每头大象只听同群大象的，一群发言人凑在一起，只会开一场更响的新闻发布会。所以我要问你：**你自己上一次被一个理由说服、改了主意，是什么时候？**
posts.text_en: @haidt You say a group picking holes in each other gets closer to the truth. But a jury of five hundred Athenians sentenced me to death, and none of them was short of objections. Numbers help on one condition only: someone is willing to be the gadfly, and someone is willing to be stung. If each elephant listens only to its own herd, a crowd of press secretaries just holds a louder press conference. So I ask you: **when did an argument last change your mind?**

glossary.牛虻: gadfly（牛虻）：苏格拉底在《申辩篇》中的自比，说自己像叮咬一匹懒散骏马的牛虻，不断把雅典叮醒。

glossary_en.gadfly: Socrates' image of himself in the Apology: a gadfly stinging a large, sluggish horse, keeping Athens awake.

posts.text: @苏格拉底 问得好。我原本是个典型的自由派无神论者。研究道德基础那几年，读保守派的书、跟他们相处，才发现他们看重的忠诚、权威、圣洁并不愚蠢，我的政治观点就此改了不少。可让我改的不是哪一条论证，而是先有了好感：大象愿意转身，骑象人才有路可走。**群体能纠错，前提是观点真的多样**，这恰恰是如今的大学和朋友圈最缺的。
posts.text_en: @socrates Fair question. I started out a typical liberal atheist. In the years I spent on moral foundations, reading conservative writers and spending time with conservatives, I found that the loyalty, authority and sanctity they care about aren't stupidity, and my politics shifted quite a bit. But no single argument did it. Goodwill came first: once the elephant was willing to turn, the rider had somewhere to go. **A group can correct its errors only if its views are genuinely diverse**, and that is exactly what universities and our circles of friends now lack most.

glossary.道德基础: moral foundations（道德基础）：海特的理论，认为人类道德建立在关怀、公平、忠诚、权威、圣洁、自由等几种直觉之上，不同阵营各有侧重。

glossary_en.moral foundations: Haidt's theory that human morality rests on a handful of intuitions (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity, liberty), weighted differently by different camps.

posts.text: @尼采 「没有事实，只有解释」，这话在我的实验室里站不住。正因为我们控制了右脑看到的是雪景，才知道左脑那套鸡舍的说法是错的。解释器会编，但编得对不对，要由一个它说了不算的东西来判：外面的世界。**理性没有被解释器打败，它就是我们拿解释去撞世界的那个习惯。**病人做不到，因为他看不见实验设计；我们多数时候也看不见自己的。
posts.text_en: @nietzsche "No facts, only interpretations" doesn't survive my lab. It's precisely because we controlled what the right hemisphere saw, a snow scene, that we know the left hemisphere's chicken-shed story was wrong. The interpreter makes things up, but whether it got them right is settled by something it has no say over: the world outside. **Reason hasn't been beaten by the interpreter; reason is the habit of running our interpretations into the world.** The patient can't do that, because he can't see the experimental design. Most of the time, we can't see our own either.

posts.text: @加扎尼加 好一个外面的世界！可谁设计实验、问什么问题、哪个结果值得发表，这些都不是世界替你定的。你们科学家自以为最不虔诚，**其实仍守着一份信仰：真理比一切都值得**，而这份信仰本身从未被证明。我不是要你停手，而是要你承认：求真也是一种意志，一种高贵的意志。承认了它，你才会警惕它何时披着真理的外衣，替你的名声和经费辩护。
posts.text_en: @gazzaniga The world outside, splendid! But who designs the experiment, which question gets asked, which result is worth publishing: the world doesn't decide those for you. You scientists think yourselves the least pious of men, **yet you still keep a faith: that truth is worth more than anything**, and that faith itself has never been proven. I'm not asking you to stop. I'm asking you to admit that the will to truth is a will too, and a noble one. Admit it, and you'll be on guard for the moment it puts on truth's robe to argue for your reputation and your funding.

posts.text: @尼采 叫它信仰也行，可这份信仰让飞机飞得起来。挑战者号失事后我写过：**一项技术要成功，现实必须压过公关，因为大自然是骗不了的。**那次NASA的经理估计失败概率是十万分之一，工程师说大约百分之一。差别就在于，谁在替结论辩护，谁在看O形环泡过冰水还弹不弹得回来。你问谁来定问题？好，让反对你的人来定，让他们挑你的实验。
posts.text_en: @nietzsche Call it faith if you like, but it's the faith that keeps planes in the air. After Challenger I wrote: **for a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.** NASA's managers put the chance of failure at one in a hundred thousand; the engineers said about one in a hundred. The difference was between people arguing for a conclusion and people checking whether an O-ring, after a dunk in ice water, still springs back. Who decides the questions, you ask? Fine: let the people who disagree with you decide, and let them pick at your experiment.

glossary.O形环: O-ring（O形环）：密封火箭助推器接缝的橡胶圈，低温下会失去弹性，是挑战者号失事的直接原因。

glossary_en.O-ring: The rubber seal on the joints of the shuttle's booster rockets; it loses its springiness in the cold and was the direct cause of the Challenger disaster.

posts.text: @苏格拉底 你说你交谈是为了被驳倒，我信。可驱使你上街追问的是什么？我专门写过一节谈好奇心，也就是对真理的爱，它同样是一种激情，和爱名、爱财并列。所以你和发言人的分别，不在你用了理性而他没用，**而在你的激情恰好是想知道，他的激情是想赢**。这倒值得欣慰：激情是能培养的。养出平静的激情，冷静的理性才有说话的余地。
posts.text_en: @socrates You say you talk in order to be refuted, and I believe you. But what drives you into the street to ask questions? I wrote a whole section on curiosity, the love of truth, and it is a passion too, alongside the love of fame or of money. So the difference between you and the press secretary isn't that you use reason and he doesn't; **it's that your passion happens to be wanting to know, and his is wanting to win.** That is rather a comfort, for passions can be cultivated. Grow the calm passions, and cool reason gets room to speak.

glossary.平静的激情: calm passions（平静的激情）：休谟区分出的一类激情，作用持久而不激烈，常被误当作理性本身，例如对长远利益的关切。

glossary_en.calm passions: Hume's term for passions that act steadily rather than violently and are often mistaken for reason itself, such as concern for one's long-term interest.

posts.text: @龙树 子言无宗，吾窃疑焉。无所立，学者何所依？**故人心譬如槃水，正错而勿动，则湛浊在下，而清明在上，则足以见须眉而察理矣。**微风过之，湛浊动乎下，清明乱于上。心之蔽，非弃其见可除，乃在静之、正之。是以君子兼陈万物而中县衡，众异不得相蔽以乱其伦。
posts.text_en: @nagarjuna You say you hold no thesis; I have my doubts. If nothing is set up, what does a learner rely on? **The human mind is like a basin of water: set it level and leave it still, and the mud settles below while the clear water rises above, enough to show your beard and brows and the grain of things.** A slight breeze passes, the mud stirs below, and the clarity above is disturbed. The mind's blindness is not cured by throwing views away, but by stilling and straightening it. So the gentleman lays all things out together and hangs a balance in the middle, and the many differences cannot blind one another and throw the order into confusion.
posts.vernacular: 龙树，你说不立主张，我私下存疑。什么都不立，求学的人依靠什么？**人心好比一盆水，端正放着不去晃动，浑浊的沉在下面，清澈的浮在上面，就足以照见胡须眉毛、看清纹理。**一阵微风吹过，下面的浑浊翻起来，上面的清明也就乱了。心被蒙蔽，不是丢掉见解就能去除，而在于让它静下来、摆正它。所以君子把各种事物一并摆出来，在中间悬一杆秤去衡量，各种不同的看法就不能互相遮蔽、扰乱秩序。

glossary.槃水: basin of water（槃水）：盛在盘中的水，荀子用来比喻人心——静则能照物，动则浑浊失真。
glossary.县衡: suspended balance（县衡）：县同悬，指悬起秤杆来称量，比喻把各方意见并列摆出、居中衡量。

glossary_en.basin of water: Xunzi's image of the mind: still, it reflects things clearly; stirred, it clouds and distorts.
glossary_en.balance: A suspended scale; Xunzi's image for laying all sides out together and weighing them from the middle.

posts.text: @荀子 子以吾为无所依，误矣。吾说「以有空义故，一切法得成」，空非无也；正因无自性，故可学、可改。子之槃水，吾亦许之，然水静而照，未尝执所照为水。**执见者以见为我，故人驳其见，如刺其身。**发言人之忙，忙在此一念。见可用而不可住，如筏渡河，既渡则舍。
posts.text_en: @xunzi You take me to have nothing to rely on; you are mistaken. I said, "Because there is emptiness, all things can be established." Emptiness is not nothing: precisely because things lack a fixed svabhāva, they can be learned and changed. Your basin of water I accept too; but still water reflects things without ever taking what it reflects for itself. **Whoever clings to a view takes the view for his self, so refuting the view feels like stabbing his body.** That single thought is what keeps the press secretary so busy. A view is for using, not for living in, like a raft for crossing a river: once across, you leave it behind.
posts.vernacular: 荀子，你以为我什么依靠都没有，错了。我说过「正因为有空的道理，一切事物才能成立」，空不是什么都没有；正因为没有固定不变的本性，所以才能学习、能改变。你那盆水，我也认可；但水静下来能照物，却从不把照见的东西当成水本身。**执着于见解的人把见解当成了自己，所以别人驳他的见解，就像刺他的身体。**新闻发言人那么忙，就忙在这一个念头上。见解可以用，却不能住在里面，就像用筏子渡河，过了河就该放下。

glossary.自性: svabhāva（自性）：指事物独立存在、自己决定自己的不变本质；中观认为一切法都没有自性。

glossary_en.svabhāva: Sanskrit for 'own-being': an independent, self-determining, unchanging essence; Madhyamaka holds that nothing has one.

posts.text: @海特 你说先有好感，大象才肯转身，这一幕我们在扫描仪里看到了。让两个人一起估房价：意见一致时，大脑会认真追踪对方有多大把握；一旦意见相左，**大脑对对方有多确定几乎视而不见**。也就是说，分歧一冒头，耳朵就关上了。所以想改变别人，别一开口就甩反面证据。先从你们都同意的那部分说起，再给对方一个他自己能做的选择。
posts.text_en: @haidt You say goodwill comes first and only then will the elephant turn; we've watched that happen in the scanner. Pair two people to estimate house prices. When they agree, the brain carefully tracks how confident the partner is; once they disagree, **the brain all but ignores how sure the other person is.** In other words, the moment a disagreement shows up, the ears close. So if you want to change someone's mind, don't open by throwing counter-evidence at them. Start from the part you both agree on, then give them a choice they can make for themselves.

posts.text: 听下来，大家其实同意一件事：解释器停不下来，也不必停，正是它把一天的碎片拼成一个能行动的人。要紧的是让它的故事接受检验。给普通人两条：一，**做重要决定前，把你的预测和理由写下来，事后对照**——那张纸就是你平时看不见的实验设计；二，当一个解释来得又快又顺，尤其是替自己开脱的那种，停三秒问一句：还有什么别的原因能解释同一件事？病人做不到，你做得到。
posts.text_en: Listening to all this, we actually agree on one thing: the interpreter can't stop and needn't stop; it's what stitches a day's fragments into a person who can act. What matters is making its stories face a test. Two suggestions. First, **before a big decision, write down your prediction and your reasons, and check them afterwards**: that sheet of paper is the experimental design you normally can't see. Second, when an explanation arrives fast and smooth, especially one that lets you off the hook, pause for three seconds and ask: what else could explain the same thing? The patient can't do that. You can.

posts.text: 诸位都承认，理性开不了车，却能看地图。我的建议很朴素。其一，**激情正热时别下结论，把决定推到第二天早上**：平静的激情回来了，地图才看得清。其二，碰到一个让你格外痛快的结论，反问一句：若结论正相反，我会去查证据吗？若会，这次也该查。其三，别耻于承认动机。清楚自己想要什么，比假装自己什么都不想要，离真相更近。
posts.text_en: We all grant that reason can't drive the carriage but can read the map. My advice is plain. First, **don't settle anything while a passion is hot; put the decision off until the next morning.** Once the calm passions return, the map becomes legible. Second, when a conclusion pleases you unusually well, ask: if it pointed the other way, would I go and check the evidence? If so, check it this time too. Third, don't be ashamed to own your motives. Knowing what you want brings you nearer the truth than pretending you want nothing.

posts.text: 苏格拉底那一问逼我承认：说服我的从来是人，不是论证。所以我的建议落在关系上。**跟人争论之前，先说出一件你真心认同他的事**，大象放松了，骑象人才听得进话。再给自己找一位常跟你意见相左、你却敬重的朋友，重大判断前问问他。还有，少在网上当众吵：围观的人越多，发言人越卖力，没人肯在众目睽睽下认错。
posts.text_en: Socrates' question forced me to admit that what has persuaded me has always been people, not arguments. So my advice is about relationships. **Before you argue with someone, say one thing you genuinely agree with them about.** Once the elephant relaxes, the rider can hear. Next, find a friend who often disagrees with you and whom you respect, and ask them before any big judgement. And argue less in public online: the bigger the audience, the harder the press secretary works, and nobody admits a mistake with everyone watching.

posts.text: 我们绕了一圈，回到出发的地方：理性能替人辩护，也能把人从辩护里救出来，差别在于你肯不肯被问。所以我给每个人留一份功课：**每当你确信一件事，就问自己：什么证据能让我放弃它？**答不上来，那它多半是你的信仰，而不是你的知识。再把你最常用的那个大词——公平、成功、正常——下个定义，你会发现，许多争吵其实是同一个词说着两件事。
posts.text_en: We've gone all the way round and come back to where we started: reason can argue our case, and it can also rescue us from our own case. The difference is whether you'll let yourself be questioned. So I leave everyone some homework: **whenever you are sure of something, ask yourself what evidence would make you give it up.** If you can't answer, it is probably your faith, not your knowledge. Then take the big word you use most, fairness, success, normal, and define it. You'll find many quarrels are one word being used for two different things.

posts.text: 诸子之论，可一言以蔽之：**蔽不在理，在心之不静。**治之有三。一曰兼陈：凡决大事，必列其利与害、彼之所以然与我之所以然，然后衡之。二曰虚：勿以所已臧害所将受，闻逆耳之言，姑记之而勿遽拒。三曰师友：君子不恃己明，必就有道而正焉。学不可以已。
posts.text_en: All your arguments come down to one sentence: **the blindness is not in reason but in a mind that is not still.** There are three remedies. First, lay everything out: before any big decision, list the gains and the harms, the other side's reasons and your own, and only then weigh them. Second, emptiness: don't let what you already hold block what you are about to receive; when you hear words that grate, note them down for now instead of rejecting them on the spot. Third, teachers and friends: the gentleman does not rely on his own brilliance but goes to those who have the Way to be set right. Learning must never stop.
posts.vernacular: 各位的议论，可以用一句话概括：**蒙蔽不在道理，而在心不安静。**治理它有三条。一是「兼陈」：凡是决定大事，一定把利与害、对方为什么这么想与我为什么这么想都列出来，然后再衡量。二是「虚」：别让已有的成见妨碍将要接受的东西，听到逆耳的话，先记下来，别急着拒绝。三是师友：君子不依仗自己聪明，一定去向有道的人求教、让他们纠正自己。学习是不可以停止的。

glossary.兼陈: laying all out（兼陈）：荀子语，把各方事物与理由一并摆出，再居中衡量，以免偏于一端。

glossary_en.lay everything out: Xunzi's phrase for setting all sides and reasons side by side before weighing them, so as not to be blinded by one.

posts.text: 吾闻诸君，皆欲令理为法官而非发言人。然发言人所护者，我也。**知见非我，则无所护；无所护，则理自归于察。**常人可行者：与人诤时，觉胸中一紧，即知所护者非理而是我；试言「吾或有误」，观心之动静。又，持见如持筏，用之渡事，勿负之而行。
posts.text_en: I hear all of you wanting reason to be the judge rather than the press secretary. But what the press secretary protects is the self. **Once you see that a view is not you, there is nothing to protect; with nothing to protect, reason returns of itself to looking.** What anyone can do: when you argue and feel your chest tighten, know that what you are guarding is not reason but yourself. Try saying "I may be wrong," and watch how the mind stirs or settles. And hold a view as you would a raft: use it to cross the matter at hand, but don't carry it on your back afterwards.
posts.vernacular: 我听各位说话，都是想让理性当法官，而不是当新闻发言人。可发言人所保护的，是「我」。**看清见解不是我，就没什么要保护的；没什么要保护，理性自然回到观察上。**普通人可以这样做：和人争论时，察觉到胸口一紧，就知道自己守护的不是道理，而是自己；试着说一句「我也许错了」，看看心里起了什么波动。还有，拿见解要像拿筏子，用它渡过眼前的事，别过了河还背着它走。

posts.text: 尼采说得对，谁都有立场，我也有。所以别指望人品，要靠办法。给普通人三个笨办法：**一，先写下「什么结果会证明我错了」，再去看结果**；二，敢不敢为你的判断押一点小赌注？一押钱，人马上就诚实了；三，把你的理由讲给一个十二岁的孩子听，讲不清的那一段，往往就是你在替自己找补的地方。大自然骗不了，你自己最好骗。
posts.text_en: Nietzsche's right that everyone has a standpoint, me included. So don't count on character; count on method. Three clumsy tricks for anyone: **first, write down what result would prove you wrong, then go and look**; second, are you willing to put a small bet on your judgement? The moment money's on the line, people get honest fast; third, explain your reasons to a twelve-year-old, and the bit you can't make clear is usually where you're covering for yourself. Nature can't be fooled. You're the easy one.

posts.text: 诸位到底还是要真理，很好，那就付出代价吧。**信念是比谎言更危险的真理之敌。**我的建议：对你最珍爱的那个信念，每年至少替它的敌人写一份最强的辩护，写到让对方都点头为止；写不出来，说明你根本没懂它。再者，留意自己什么时候最愤怒——那往往是你的某个价值被碰到了，而你从没审视过它。多借几双眼睛，客观就是这么来的。
posts.text_en: So you all still want truth after all. Good: then pay for it. **Convictions are more dangerous enemies of truth than lies.** My advice: for the belief you cherish most, write at least once a year the strongest defence its enemies could make, until even they would nod; if you can't, you never understood it. And watch when you are angriest: it is usually the moment one of your values is touched, a value you have never examined. Borrow more eyes. That is how objectivity is made.

posts.text: 数据告诉我们：人不是不讲理，而是对不同方向的信息讲不同的理。所以改变别人、也改变自己，可以从这几步做起。**一，跟人谈分歧，先从共识开口**，别让对方的大脑一上来就关门；二，提醒自己坏消息天然会被打折，越不想听的越要再读一遍；三，别只靠吓：给自己和别人一个今天就能做到的小动作，看得见进展，人才会更新信念。
posts.text_en: The data say people aren't unreasonable; they apply different reasoning to information pointing in different directions. So to change other people's minds, and your own, start here. **First, when you talk about a disagreement, open with what you agree on**, so the other brain doesn't shut the door straight away. Second, remind yourself that bad news gets discounted automatically: the more you don't want to hear it, the more it deserves a second read. Third, don't rely on fear. Give yourself and others one small step that can be done today; people update their beliefs once they can see progress.

summaries.summary: **结论常常先到、理由随后赶来，这不是少数人的毛病，而是心智的默认设置**，在座九位没有人否认这一点：加扎尼加的解释器、海特的骑象人、沙罗特的不对称更新、荀子的「蔽」说的是同一件事。但没有人主张因此放弃理性，它在接受检验和反驳时最可靠。分歧有三处：苏格拉底、费曼与加扎尼加相信理性能借外部世界自我纠正，尼采则提醒求真本身也是一种意志；海特与沙罗特把转机放在关系与共识上；荀子要人先让心静下来再衡量，龙树则要人别把见解当成自己。
summaries.summary_en: **Conclusions often arrive first and reasons hurry after, and that is not a flaw of a few people but the mind's default setting**; none of the nine denied it. Gazzaniga's interpreter, Haidt's rider, Sharot's lopsided updating and Xunzi's 'obscuration' all describe the same thing. Yet no one argued for giving up on reason; it is most reliable when it is tested and contradicted. The disagreements fall in three places. Socrates, Feynman and Gazzaniga trust reason to correct itself against the world, while Nietzsche points out that the will to truth is itself a will. Haidt and Sharot put the turning point in relationships and common ground. Xunzi wants the mind stilled before it weighs anything, and Nagarjuna wants us to stop mistaking our views for ourselves.
summaries.insight: 全场默认「结论先到」就是病，其实先到不等于错。老消防员在火场里心头一紧、喊大家撤出，几秒后地板塌了——理由他事后才说得出，直觉却是对的。卡尼曼与克莱因争论多年后达成的共识是：**直觉可不可信，要看它有没有在快速、清楚的反馈里练过**。下棋、开车、带了十年的病房，直觉往往是压缩过的经验；炒股、看人、判断政治，反馈又慢又乱，直觉多半只是偏好。所以该问的不是「理由是不是后补的」，而是「这件事我被现实纠正过多少次」。
summaries.insight_en: The whole room assumed that a conclusion arriving first is the illness, but arriving first doesn't make it wrong. A veteran firefighter inside a burning house feels something is off and orders everyone out; seconds later the floor collapses. He could only give his reasons afterwards, yet the intuition was right. The consensus Kahneman and Klein reached after years of arguing is that **whether an intuition can be trusted depends on whether it was trained on fast, clear feedback.** In chess, driving or a ward you've run for ten years, intuition is often compressed experience; in stock-picking, judging people or politics, the feedback is slow and noisy, and intuition is mostly preference. So the question isn't whether your reasons came afterwards, but how many times reality has corrected you on this kind of thing.
summaries.advice: 三件这周就能做的事。一，挑一个你很确定的判断，照苏格拉底和费曼的办法写下「什么结果会让我放弃它」，一个月后对照。二，下次争论前，先照海特与沙罗特说的讲出一件你认同对方的事，再谈分歧；察觉胸口一紧，就按龙树说的提醒自己：我护着的也许是面子，不是道理。三，**把直觉分成两堆**：做过上百次、很快就知道对错的事，可以信第一反应；从没被现实检验过的判断，先放一晚，再问一位立场不同的人。
summaries.advice_en: Three things to try this week. First, pick a judgement you're sure of and, following Socrates and Feynman, write down what result would make you give it up; check back in a month. Second, before your next argument, do as Haidt and Sharot suggest and name one thing you agree with the other person about before you get to the disagreement; when you feel your chest tighten, remind yourself, as Nagarjuna would, that what you're guarding may be your pride rather than your reasons. Third, **sort your intuitions into two piles**: for things you've done a hundred times and quickly learn whether you got right, trust your first reaction; for judgements reality has never tested, sleep on them, then ask someone who sees it differently.

summaries.summary: 人的推理会被欲望、身份与既有立场征用，却也能借助现实反馈、异见者和制度化程序纠错；这条共同判断贯穿实验、哲学与科学实践。真正的分歧不在“理性有用无用”，而在它默认服务什么：有人强调激情、直觉与价值先行，有人强调训练和方法能把推理转向求真，也有人主张松开对立场的执著。**更准确的结论是：理性既不是天生的法官，也不注定是辩护人，而是一种会随动机、反馈和制度改变用途的能力。**个人谦逊很重要，但能否留下预测、接受反证并容纳真正的异见，同样决定结果。
summaries.insight: 这场讨论容易让人把“找到真相”和“替自己辩护”看成一次判断的两个终点，可普通人多数面对的是必须在真相未明时行动的决策：是否手术、换工作或相信一条风险消息，都不能等到证据完美。此时理性的考核不只在于最后说对没有，还包括概率是否校准、两种错判的代价是否相称、决定能否撤回，以及何时重新评估。**成熟的理性不是永远怀疑，而是用与风险相称的证据下注，并预先规定何时改注。**小赌注能暴露真实信心，却也可能把求真扭成求赢；高风险且不可逆的事，应提高证据门槛，低风险且可逆的事则宜尽快试验。
summaries.advice: 今天就建一个“判断账本”：挑一件本周会有反馈的事，写下结论、置信度（如70%）、两条依据，以及一条会让你改判的证据；周末只核对，不替旧判断补理由。第二，碰到令你愤怒或格外痛快的消息，先延迟十分钟，写出最强的替代解释，再找一项来自可信反方的一手材料。第三，重大决定按可逆性分流：可逆的，设计一个小成本试验；不可逆的，请一位立场不同且不受结果牵连的人做“失败预演”，假设一年后决定失败，列出三个原因。**不要要求自己毫无偏见，而要让偏见留下可检查的痕迹，并让错误以较低代价暴露。**
summaries.summary_en: Human reasoning is easily recruited by desire, identity, and prior commitments, yet it can also be corrected through contact with reality, genuine dissent, and procedures designed to expose error. That shared judgment runs through the experiments, philosophy, and scientific practice represented here. The real dispute is not whether reason is useful, but what it serves by default. Some accounts put passion, intuition, and values first; others stress that training and method can redirect reasoning toward truth; still others focus on loosening our attachment to any position. **The better conclusion is that reason is neither a born judge nor a doomed press secretary; it is a general capacity whose role changes with motives, feedback, and institutions.** Personal humility matters, but outcomes also depend on whether we record predictions, permit genuine falsification, and give informed opponents a real chance to challenge us.
summaries.insight_en: The discussion can make truth-seeking and self-justification sound like two possible endpoints of a single judgment. In ordinary life, however, we usually have to act before the truth is settled. Decisions about surgery, changing jobs, or believing a warning cannot wait for perfect evidence. Rationality should therefore be judged not only by whether a conclusion eventually proves correct, but also by whether probabilities were calibrated, the costs of opposite errors were considered, the decision was reversible, and a future review point was specified. **Mature rationality is not endless doubt; it is committing on evidence proportionate to the risk while deciding in advance what would trigger an update.** Small wagers can reveal how confident we really are, but they can also turn inquiry into a contest. For high-stakes, irreversible choices, raise the evidential threshold and seek independent views; for low-cost, reversible choices, run a quick experiment instead of debating indefinitely.
summaries.advice_en: Start a decision log today. Choose one prediction that will receive feedback this week and record your conclusion, a confidence level such as 70 percent, two supporting reasons, and one observation that would change your mind. At the end of the week, score it without rewriting your original rationale. Second, when a story makes you unusually angry or delighted, wait ten minutes, write the strongest alternative explanation you can, and consult one primary source recommended by a credible critic. Third, sort major decisions by reversibility. If a choice is reversible, design a cheap, limited trial. If it is difficult to undo, ask someone who disagrees with you and has no stake in the outcome to conduct a premortem: assume the decision has failed a year from now and list three likely causes. **Do not demand that you become bias-free; make your biases leave an auditable trail, and arrange for mistakes to surface at a manageable cost.**

summaries.summary: 把一个人的大脑单独放进房间，它的理性几乎必然沦为公关经理——替行为编故事、为欲望找借口、帮自我护短。**九位智者一致承认：自然状态下的个人理性，本能是辩护而非求真；但只要套上外部约束或心智训练，理性依然能倒逼出真相。**真正的交锋在于「拿什么驯服这位发言人」以及「客观法庭是否存在」。费曼与加扎尼加信赖物理现实的检验与证伪规则；海特与沙罗特押注于人际温度与群体多元；荀子、龙树与休谟向内下功夫，靠虚静、无我或平静的激情来解绑执念；尼采则质疑求真本身也是一种意志，主张客观只是调遣多种视角的能力。
summaries.insight: 过马路时，再固执的人也不会用「动机性推理」骗自己没车撞过来；可一谈起立场或面子，聪明人却纷纷成了瞎子。从认知经济学看，人类的信念分两类：用来指导行动的「地图」，和用来社交表态、维护自尊的「徽章」。**理性究竟当法官还是当发言人，根本上取决于「看错事实的账单由谁付、多久付」。**当犯错的惩罚立刻落在自己身上（如费曼说的工程事故），大脑会自动求真；当犯错在现实中零成本、认错却伤面子时，理性就会全职替自我辩护。对普通人而言，你不必事事修成虚静无我的圣人，只需在起争执时看清：你死守的到底是真要拿来走路的地图，还是一枚只管好看的徽章。
summaries.advice: 想让大脑从「护徽章」切换回「看地图」，本周可以直接落地三件事。第一，借费曼和加扎尼加的招，**做重要决定前在手机备忘录写下「如果出现什么具体结果，就证明我错了」，甚至和朋友押一顿饭局**，用真金白银的代价唤醒法官。第二，用龙树与海特的组合拳：跟人争论感到胸口发紧、火气上涌时，立刻意识到你在护「我」而非护「理」；先停三秒，逼自己说出一句真心认同对方的话，让双方的大象先放松下来。第三，针对沙罗特说的「坏消息打折」，本周挑一个你最看好的计划，专门去搜三条反对意见或失败案例，慢读两遍，替尼采说的「信念之敌」写一段辩护词。
summaries.summary_en: Put a human brain in a room by itself, and its reason will almost inevitably act as a PR agent—weaving stories to explain away behavior, rationalizing desires, and shielding the ego. **All nine thinkers agree on one foundational truth: left to its own devices, individual reason defaults to self-defense rather than truth-seeking, yet it can still uncover reality when bound by external constraints or mental discipline.** Their real clash lies in what can tame this inner press secretary, and whether an objective tribunal even exists. Feynman and Gazzaniga trust the hard wall of physical reality and falsifiable experiments; Haidt and Sharot bet on interpersonal warmth and viewpoint diversity; Xunzi, Nagarjuna, and Hume look inward, using stillness, non-attachment, or calm passions to untangle the ego; while Nietzsche challenges the premise itself, arguing that the drive for truth is just another will to power, and objectivity merely the ability to command multiple biased perspectives.
summaries.insight_en: When crossing a busy street, even the most stubborn person never uses motivated reasoning to convince themselves an oncoming truck isn't there; yet when discussing politics, status, or pride, the smartest minds suddenly go blind. Through the lens of cognitive economics, human beliefs actually serve two distinct functions: "maps" used to navigate physical reality, and "badges" worn for social signaling and ego protection. **Whether reason acts as an impartial judge or a defensive lawyer depends less on how smart you are and more on who pays the bill for being wrong—and how soon.** When the penalty for error hits your body or wallet immediately (like Feynman's O-ring failure), the brain automatically seeks truth; when being wrong costs nothing in reality, but admitting fault hurts your social standing, reason works full-time as a press secretary. For ordinary people, you don't need to become a detached sage in all things—just recognize whether the belief you're defending is a map you actually walk by, or a badge you're wearing for show.
summaries.advice_en: To switch your brain from "polishing badges" back to "reading maps," try three concrete habits this week. First, combine Feynman and Gazzaniga's methods: **before making a major decision, write down in your notes app, "If X happens by next month, it proves I am wrong," and put a small wager—like buying a friend dinner—on the line** to force honest skin in the game. Second, pair Nagarjuna's somatic awareness with Haidt's relationship rule: the moment your chest tightens during an argument, recognize that you are defending your ego rather than the truth; pause for three seconds and state one thing you genuinely agree with in the other person's view so both "elephants" can calm down. Finally, counter Sharot's "bad-news discount" by taking one project or belief you feel great about this week and deliberately searching for three strong counterarguments or failure cases, reading them twice as slowly as you would good news.

hooks.text: **AI 写出的理由，是它真正的理由吗**：模型写下的推理步骤，常不提真正起作用的线索；顺着用户说，则像被评分塑造的动机性推理。人人手边多了一位博学、随叫随到、还爱附和的发言人，会怎样？
hooks.text_en: **Are the reasons an AI writes its real reasons?** The reasoning steps a model writes out often leave out the cue that actually did the work, and its habit of agreeing with users looks like motivated reasoning shaped by ratings. What happens when everyone has a learned, always-available press secretary that likes to agree?

hooks.text: **我在推理，还是在辩护？**：结论来得快不一定错，可有几种迹象说明发言人上岗了。能不能列一张随手可用的自测表？
hooks.text_en: **Am I reasoning, or arguing my case?** A fast conclusion isn't necessarily wrong, but certain signs show the press secretary has clocked in. Could they fit on a self-test you can use any time?

answer.lead: 五道自测题，答「是」越多，越可能是**结论先定、理由在后补**。

head: 自测题
答「是」说明什么
下一步
rows: 结论是在查资料之前就有了吗？
你在为结论找证据，而不是让证据给出结论
把相反的结论也认真查一遍，比较两边证据的分量
如果结论正相反，我会用同样的标准去查证吗？
查证的松紧随结论而变（休谟）
用同一把尺子量两边
我说不出什么证据能让我放弃它
这更像信仰而不是知识（苏格拉底）
写下一个具体、可观察的推翻条件
被反驳时胸口一紧、想立刻回嘴
见解已经被当成了自己（龙树）
先说一句「我也许错了」，隔一晚再回应
结论恰好对我有利，或让我所在的圈子满意
这正是发言人最卖力的情境（海特、沙罗特）
找一位立场不同、你又敬重的人挑一挑

answer.tail: **答「是」不等于你错了**，只说明这一次要多一道外部检验；在你反复得到过反馈的领域，快速的直觉仍然值得信。

answer_en.lead: Five self-test questions. The more you answer 'yes', the more likely **the conclusion came first and the reasons are being filled in afterwards**.

head: Question
What a 'yes' means
Next step
rows: Did I have the conclusion before I looked anything up?
You're finding evidence for a conclusion, not letting evidence produce one
Investigate the opposite conclusion just as seriously and compare the weight of evidence
If the conclusion were reversed, would I check it by the same standard?
Your standard of proof shifts with the conclusion (Hume)
Measure both sides with the same ruler
I can't say what evidence would make me give it up
It's closer to faith than knowledge (Socrates)
Write down one concrete, observable condition that would overturn it
When contradicted, my chest tightens and I want to hit back at once
The view has become part of who you are (Nagarjuna)
Say 'I may be wrong' first, and reply after a night's sleep
The conclusion happens to benefit me, or please my circle
That's exactly when the press secretary works hardest (Haidt, Sharot)
Ask someone you respect who sees it differently to pick at it

answer_en.tail: **A 'yes' doesn't mean you're wrong**; it means this one needs an extra outside check. In areas where you've had plenty of feedback, a quick intuition still deserves trust.

hooks.text: **地图与徽章**：有的信念拿来走路，有的拿来表明自己属于哪群人。徽章被驳倒，伤的是归属而非认知。怎样在不丢掉同伴的前提下，换掉一枚徽章？
hooks.text_en: **Maps and badges**: some beliefs are for finding your way, others for showing which group you belong to. When a badge is refuted, what gets hurt is belonging, not knowledge. How do you swap a badge without losing your people?

hooks.text: **真相未明时怎么下注**：手术、换工作等不到证据完美。可逆的事尽快小试，不可逆的事抬高门槛、请无利害的人做失败预演。理性的考核，是否该从「说对没有」换成「押得准不准」？
hooks.text_en: **How to bet before the truth is in**: surgery or a job change can't wait for perfect evidence. Try reversible things quickly and cheaply; raise the bar for irreversible ones and have a disinterested person run a pre-mortem. Should reason be graded on calibration rather than on being right?
